content: Healthcare providers should focus on building capacity for counseling and managing post-dose vomiting, as well as understanding when redosing is necessary. Additionally, they should provide guidance on using food to mask the taste of medications. Tuberculosis (TB) Preventive Treatment (TPT): 1. Systematic Data Recording and Reporting: Strengthen the systematic recording and reporting of TB preventive treatment data, either through case forms or electronic platforms. Key data variables should be integrated into the Health Management Information System (HMIS) to facilitate monitoring and evaluation of performance. 2. Baseline Assessment for TPT Initiation: Once active TB disease is ruled out and a decision is made to consider TPT, a baseline assessment should be conducted to determine the individual’s eligibility. This includes: Personal History: Collect information on allergies or hypersensitivity to TB drugs (e.g., isoniazid, rifampicin, rifabutin, rifapentine), HIV status and antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen, pregnancy status or contraceptive use, comorbidities (e.g., malnutrition, diabetes, viral hepatitis), and medications being taken. Assess for potential contraindications to TPT, such as active hepatitis, elevated liver enzymes (>3x upper limit of normal), heavy alcohol use, or symptoms of peripheral neuropathy. These conditions require detailed investigations and clinical judgment to weigh the risks and benefits of TPT. Medication History: Review the individual’s medication history to guide the choice of TPT regimen or adjust treatment for comorbid conditions. Certain drug classes, such as antiretrovirals (ARVs), opioids, and antimalarials, may interact with TPT. Liver Function Testing (LFT): Routine baseline LFT is not mandatory unless risk factors (e.g., history of liver disease, alcohol use, HIV infection, pregnancy, or postpartum period) are present. If baseline LFT results are abnormal, clinical judgment is required to determine whether the benefits of TPT outweigh the risks. Routine LFT during treatment is encouraged for individuals with additional risk factors. 3. Counseling and Support: Counseling should include: Explaining the rationale and benefits of TPT for the individual, household, and community. Providing information on the prescribed TPT regimen, including duration, medication instructions, and follow-up schedules. Discussing potential side effects and adverse events, and advising on steps to take if they occur. Emphasizing the importance of completing the full course of TPT. Agreeing on a treatment adherence plan, including the most suitable location for drug intake (home, community, or health facility) and whether a treatment supporter is needed. Digital tools, such as video-observed treatment (VOT) or SMS reminders, may also be used to support adherence. 4. Adherence to TPT: Adherence to the TPT regimen is critical for achieving clinical benefits. Poor adherence or early cessation of TPT can reduce its protective efficacy and potentially increase the risk of developing TB, including drug-resistant TB. Studies suggest that taking at least 80% of the prescribed doses within the recommended duration is essential for effective TB prevention. 5. Monitoring During TPT: Individuals on TPT should be monitored at every healthcare contact, ideally monthly or as required by national policy. Monitoring should include: Reinforcing understanding of TB symptoms, the importance of TPT, and adherence. Checking for signs of TB disease and adverse drug reactions. Adjusting dosages based on weight, especially in children, as rapid weight gain may require dosage changes. Managing comorbid conditions and consulting specialists when necessary. Recording all findings and drug intake in individual case files. 6. Special Populations: Pregnant and Postpartum Women: Pregnant women living with HIV are at higher risk for TB. TPT can be initiated during pregnancy or postpartum with appropriate care. Routine LFT is not required unless other risks are present. Vitamin B6 supplementation should be provided to all pregnant and breastfeeding women on TPT. Rifampicin is generally safe during pregnancy, and no dose adjustment is needed. Breastfeeding Women: Preventive treatment with isoniazid or rifampicin can be safely given to breastfeeding women. Infants of mothers on TPT should receive supplemental pyridoxine (Vitamin B6). Women on Hormonal Contraceptives: Rifampicin and rifapentine may reduce the efficacy of oral and hormonal contraceptives. Women should consider alternative contraceptive methods, such as depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) or barrier methods, in consultation with a clinician. Individuals with Liver Disease: TPT should be initiated cautiously in individuals with elevated liver enzymes (>3x upper limit of normal) and avoided in those with end-stage liver disease. However, isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) is generally well-tolerated in individuals with chronic hepatitis B or C. Renal Failure: Isoniazid and rifampicin are eliminated via biliary excretion and can be given in standard doses to patients with renal failure. Pyridoxine should be co-administered to prevent peripheral neuropathy. 7. Contacts of Drug-Resistant TB Patients: Household contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or isoniazid mono-resistance are at higher risk of TB infection. Preventive treatment options may include fluoroquinolones, along with other TB agents like ethambutol or ethionamide, if tolerated. Clinical follow-up for two years is recommended to monitor for signs of TB disease. 8. Integration with Differentiated Service Delivery (DSD): TPT services should be integrated into DSD models for HIV care, which aim to reduce the burden on healthcare facilities and improve patient convenience. These models can include community-based ART distribution, adherence clubs, and remote medication pick-ups. TPT regimens of any length can be provided under DSD, with mechanisms in place to manage adverse events and document TPT indicators systematically. 9. Key Considerations for Scale-Up: National programs should align TPT scale-up with transitions to newer ART regimens, such as dolutegravir-based therapies. This provides an opportunity to integrate TPT into routine care and generate implementation experience for broader national adoption. 10. Ethical Principles: Individuals should not feel coerced into taking TPT. Informed decisions to decline or discontinue treatment should be respected.
